description: A team interested in using NASA satellite data to understand harmful algal blooms and environmental change. Our goal is to build a useful tool that visualizes trends and tests whether changes are statistically meaningful. Looking for teammates interested in web development, data analysis, statistics, or design.
summary:
Our goal: catch cyanobacteria blooms in Florida lakes before they form, so managers can act while prevention is still cheap, instead of paying for closures, treatment and restoration once a bloom takes hold.

First we asked whether today's tools can give that warning. Using NASA-archived satellite bloom data (CyAN), NASA MERRA-2 temperature and rainfall, and 26,629 field water samples across 121 lakes, we tested EPA's weekly bloom forecast, including the moment that matters most: the week a clear lake turns into a bloom.

What we found: graded against satellite labels, the forecast helped mainly for cheap early actions on lakes not yet blooming. Graded against independent field samples, it ranked lakes no better than last week's satellite view. The satellite record also reads higher every year for the same field chlorophyll, so any early-warning system must be checked against field data, not satellite data alone.

Our tool shows each lake's satellite, field and NASA climate records side by side with trend and significance tests. Next: an onset model driven by warning signs (temperature, nutrients, rainfall) plus real intervention costs, to show where acting early saves money.
details:
What it does

Bloom Trend Detective is a free, public tool for checking whether a satellite bloom trend for a Florida lake is real. It works in four steps:

  1. Pick a lake. Choose one of 121 Florida lakes from a map or a list.
  2. Pick a variable. Satellite bloom weeks (share of May-October weeks the satellite flagged as blooming), satellite bloom extent (share of the lake's area above the bloom threshold), field chlorophyll (what boats and volunteers measured in water samples), or NASA MERRA-2 warm-season air temperature and rainfall.
  3. Get a verdict. The yearly series with its trend line, the rate of change with a 95% range, the p-value, and one of three verdicts: "Significant upward/downward trend", "Possible trend, not significant after accounting for testing many lakes", or "No clear trend yet".
  4. Get a second opinion. For lakes with both records, the tool says whether the satellite and the field samples point the same way over 2020-2025, and how well they agree year to year.

A statewide section lays the whole thing out as a case: two witnesses (satellite and field), the evidence, and the suspects.

What we found

  • The satellite says rising. Averaged over lakes, the share of warm-season weeks flagged as blooming went from 11% in 2020 to 30% in 2026.
  • Field samples agree on direction. Field chlorophyll rose a median 7.5% per year over 2020-2025 (95% CI 2.6 to 13.2; 45 lakes).
  • But the satellite reads higher every year for the same field chlorophyll: +2.5 points of bloom extent per year (95% CI 1.4 to 3.6; 2,541 same-week matchups in 106 lakes). Field chlorophyll eased after 2023 while the satellite kept climbing.
  • Verdict. The rise through 2023 looks real. The climb since then is not confirmed. Three suspects remain: instrument or processing drift, a real shift toward cyanobacteria that total chlorophyll can't see, or a change in sampling.

From trend to decision

EPA publishes a weekly bloom forecast for these lakes. We compared it with the simplest rival, "act if the satellite showed a bloom last week", twice. Graded against satellite labels (6,980 lake-weeks), last week's view looked clearly better (Brier score 0.043 vs 0.099). Graded against field samples (506 lake-weeks in 86 lakes), there was no clear winner: ranking skill (ROC-AUC) was 0.76 for the forecast and 0.75 for last week's view. That corrected our own first result. Grading a satellite-based forecast only against satellite labels flatters the rival that uses the same instrument; field data is the fairer judge.

How it works

  • Satellite bloom labels. CyAN weekly lake histograms give the lake-median cyanobacteria index. A week counts as a bloom when the index is at least 130 (about 12 µg/L chlorophyll-a), EPA's own threshold. Weeks with less than half the lake visible are "unknown", never "no bloom".
  • Field data. Chlorophyll-a from the Water Quality Portal (Florida LAKEWATCH volunteers, FDEP, counties, water management districts). Stations are matched to lakes by their position inside the lake outline: 2,993 stations in 115 lakes, 26,629 samples.
  • Statistics. Mann-Kendall test (exact for 8 or fewer seasons), Sen's slope with a confidence interval, Benjamini-Hochberg correction across lakes, lake-resampled bootstrap intervals, and a drift model with lake and month fixed effects.
  • NASA MERRA-2. Monthly temperature and rainfall from NASA POWER, 1981-2025. All 121 lakes show significant warm-season warming, a median +0.28 °C per decade. The lakes share 26 grid cells, so this is regional air, not lake water.
  • Rules first. For every test, we wrote the rules down before computing the result (protocol amendments in the repository).

Why it matters

Satellite indicators are increasingly used to decide where to sample and when to warn the public. If a satellite trend is partly the instrument, decisions built on it go wrong quietly. Our tool gives students and residents a way to check a claim like "blooms are getting worse here" against two independent records, and gives agencies a simple, reproducible check on whether a trend is in the lakes or in the instrument.

Tools

Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn) for the analysis, with unit tests for the statistics. Plotly.js and plain HTML/CSS for a static website with no server and no login. Code: github.com/Coder-13-11/bloom-trend-detective (Apache-2.0).

What we don't claim

No toxin, health or water-safety information: the index estimates cyanobacterial chlorophyll, not toxins. No dollar savings. No claim about what causes the rise, and no claim that EPA's national forecast is wrong: we tested one state. Known limits: field samples measure total chlorophyll at points while the satellite measures a surface signal; lakes share weather, so our intervals are too narrow; and 2025-26 field data are still arriving.
